summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions that apply on the island.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold in the record; no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation appear in the sources.

Article 1:221 of the Criminal Code defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed, and no transgender-specific provision is cited.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11 to 5 (with four abstentions per the Associated Press account of 9 September 2016) to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights; the campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the July 2024 Supreme Court ruling.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that meeting acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatized as disordered.

Harassment has nonetheless occurred. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007) that forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights. The most recent documented incident of anti-LGBT harassment in this record is from that 2004–2007 period; no later instance is documented.

Several specific gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. The last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'

The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.
tangentialFactors:
Aruba is frequently called one of the Caribbean's most LGBT-friendly islands, and a GlobalGayz cultural report edited in January 2017 describes the island as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, noting Catholic influence as the main brake. The same report notes that the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and that same-sex adoption is legal.

Religious and cultural opposition to the 2016 registered-partnership vote was strong, and at that time neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions.

Local LGBT associations including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba are active, and openly-gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes introduced the registered partnership bill in August 2016.

outOfScopeNotes:
The record contains no Aruba-specific legal provision, policy or incident addressing transgender persons' identity documents, gender markers, restroom or facility access, or healthcare. The 22 April 2015 Kingdom endorsement expressly included transgender persons, but no implementing Aruba measure is sourced here. Whether the Criminal Code's discrimination provisions have ever been applied to a gender-identity complaint is not sourced.

No figure in this record measures the prevalence of violence against transgender people in Aruba against the island's general crime rate, so no comparative risk magnitude can be stated.
